analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal license, safety training, and a background check for anyone to buy or possess a gun.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on December 17, 2025 and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has had no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal to buy, receive, or own a gun without a federal license. To get one, a person would need to pass a safety course with a written and hands-on test, submit fingerprints to a full background check, and clear an investigation in which the Attorney General can deny a license to anyone judged a significant danger to themselves or others. Every gun sale — including private sales — would have to go through a licensed dealer for a background check, and sellers would have to report every transfer to the Attorney General within 3 business days. States with their own substantially similar licensing systems could be exempted.
analysis.who_benefits: The bill aims to reduce gun deaths and injuries by keeping firearms out of the hands of people judged dangerous, requiring safety training before anyone can buy a gun, and closing loopholes that allow private sales with no background check. People at elevated risk of gun violence, and communities affected by it, would benefit most if it worked as designed. Current gun owners would need licenses to keep possessing firearms, but the license is free of the training requirement only at issuance — everyone would go through the same process.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of gun violence

how_it_helps.text: It is unlawful to purchase, receive, or possess a firearm without a federal license, so anyone currently barred from buying guns cannot lawfully hold them.
Every applicant must pass a firearms safety training course with a written test and hands-on firing test, plus a full background investigation with fingerprints and proof of identity.

The Attorney General may deny or revoke a license for anyone posing a significant danger of bodily injury to self or others, based on factors like a history of violence, domestic violence or stalking orders, drug or alcohol abuse, or unsafe firearm handling.

It closes the private-sale loophole by requiring all sales between people who are not licensed dealers to go through a licensed dealer for a point-of-sale background check, and it requires every firearm sale to be reported to the Attorney General within 3 business days.

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on gun buyers and owners: a new federal license process for every purchase (one license per gun), safety training with written and firing tests, travel to a designated licensing office, and waits of up to 30 days per application. The federal government would bear the cost of running background investigations and a nationwide licensing office network, and licensed dealers would handle all private-sale transfers.

drawbacks.text: The license is valid for one firearm purchase only, must be used within 30 days, and expires after 5 years — meaning every single purchase requires a new background investigation, new fingerprints, and new waiting periods, which would be slow and costly for buyers and for the federal offices processing applications.
Applicants must travel to a designated physical office, which could be a burden in rural areas even with the requirement that offices be located in both urban and rural areas.

The 'significant danger of bodily injury' denial standard lets the Attorney General deny a license based on broad discretionary factors, including arrests without conviction, with judicial review available only after denial.
Because the bill requires a license to possess a firearm, it covers current gun owners, not just new purchasers, making it a far broader federal regulation of gun ownership than existing law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a system that could meaningfully reduce gun deaths by keeping firearms from people flagged as dangerous, closing the private-sale and ghost-gun loopholes, and requiring safety training. The costs are real and the drafters' own text acknowledges them: processing capacity is unaddressed, the 30-day windows are unenforceable as written, and universal possession licensing touches every current gun owner, making it the most restrictive federal gun proposal in Congress. The bill's fate will be decided by politics, not by design flaws alone.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and nothing has happened since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on December 17, 2025.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee; the action history shows no further steps, no hearings, and no vote.
Eight senators in total — all Democrats — introduced or cosponsored it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has not advanced, nothing has changed: current federal law's looser rules on gun purchases and private sales remain in place, which is the outcome the gun industry and gun-rights groups prefer. If it never advances, they remain better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun-rights advocates and the firearms industry

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

for.name: Sens. Kim, Schatz, Warren, Blumenthal, Schiff, Padilla, and Hirono

sides.party_line_note: All eight supporters are Democrats; no Republican support appears in the record, and Republicans hold 55 of 100 Senate seats.

industries.note: Universal licensing and dealer-mediated transfers would reduce impulse purchases, add friction to every sale, and likely shrink the number of lawful gun owners over time. The industry consistently opposes such measures through outside channels.
All private sales must run through a licensed dealer for a background check, making dealers the mandatory gatekeepers of every transfer and a source of new fee revenue.

analysis.trajectory: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where the majority party has shown no interest, and with 55 Republican senators there is no realistic path to a floor vote this Congress. Bills at this stage — introduced, one committee, no cosponsors from the majority party — almost never advance.
